claim: Sio and Ormerod 2009 meta-analysis: 117 effect sizes from 29 publications, 3,606 participants; the weighted random-effects mean incubation effect is d = 0.29 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.39).
quote: The mean of the weighted unbiased effect size was 0.29, with a standard deviation of 0.04, and the 95% confidence interval was 0.21, 0.39.
authors: Sio, U. N.; Ormerod, T. C.
title: Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
transfer: none directly; sets expectation that a delay step has a small average gain

claim: The 0.41 figure in Sio and Ormerod is the UNWEIGHTED mean of the raw unbiased effect sizes; after recoding outliers the unweighted mean is 0.36.
quote: The unweighted mean of the unbiased effect size estimate was 0.41, with a standard deviation of 0.71.
authors: Sio, U. N.; Ormerod, T. C.
title: Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
transfer: none

claim: CHECK: Incubation effect size conflict is resolved. The primary paper gives 0.41 (unweighted raw mean), 0.36 (unweighted, outliers recoded) and 0.29 (weighted random-effects, the headline estimate). Use d = 0.29, CI 0.21 to 0.39. The 0.32 in the Gilhooly et al. manuscript matches none of these and should not be cited. Neither a-16 (0.41) nor c-04 (0.29) was wrong; they report different estimators.
authors: Sio and Ormerod 2009; Gilhooly et al. manuscript (Brunel BURA 2438/9116)
title: Resolution of effect size conflict
transfer: none

claim: In Sio and Ormerod, weighted subgroup means were d = 0.22 for linguistic insight (65 studies), 0.26 for visual (35) and 0.29 for creative/divergent (14). The creative-task advantage shows in the regression (visual and linguistic coefficients negative), not as a big gap in raw subgroup means. Only 14 creative studies.
quote: The negative coefficients associated with visual problems and linguistic problems indicate that individuals solving these two types of insight problem showed a smaller incubation effect than did individuals solving creative problems.
authors: Sio, U. N.; Ormerod, T. C.
title: Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
transfer: none; incubation helps divergent work somewhat more, but on few studies

claim: CHECK: 'Incubation helps divergent tasks more than insight tasks, and more after long preparation' (a-17) is supported by the primary paper. But the divergent mean d of .65 quoted in a secondary manuscript is not in the primary paper's subgroup table (0.29 weighted). The longer-preparation effect held for visual (r=.40) and creative (r=.60) problems, not linguistic (r=.04).
quote: There was a statistically significant positive correlation between the weighted incubation effect size and the length of the preparation period with visual problems, r(35)  .40, p  .02, and creative problems, r(14)  .60, p  .03, but not with linguistic problems
authors: Sio, U. N.; Ormerod, T. C.
title: Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
transfer: none

claim: CHECK: Break demand. Sio and Ormerod found low-demand fillers beat rest only for linguistic insight problems (difference 0.45, p<.05). The high vs low demand difference pointed the same way but was not significant. So 'undemanding task beats rest' is a moderator result for one problem class, and the old a-18 vs c-05 conflict is partly a problem-type difference.
quote: Surprisingly, low cognitive demand tasks yielded a stronger incubation effect than did rest during an incubation period when solving linguistic insight problems.
authors: Sio, U. N.; Ormerod, T. C.
title: Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
transfer: none

claim: A 2025 study (n=85, Unusual Uses Task, 15-min 0-back incubation) found no significant effect of mind wandering on divergent thinking. Incubation raised fluency (d=1.03 repeated, 0.47 novel items) and originality (d=1.10, 0.52), mostly as more ideas, not better ones. The summary I opened shows no no-break control.
quote: Results revealed no significant effects of mind wandering on divergent thinking.
authors: Du, Q.; Gordon, R.; Tolmie, A.
title: The Role of Mind Wandering During Incubation in Divergent and Convergent Creative Thinking
transfer: none; a break may add more ideas on the same item, not better ones

claim: A 2025 preregistered study (story writing, 10-min break, 0-back vs 2-back vs mindfulness vs no break) found no difference in creative improvement between incubation tasks. More self-reported mind wandering predicted more improvement in semantic-distance creativity, only when the same prompt was reused. GPT-4 ratings supported it.
authors: McDaniel, C.; Habibi, A.; Kaplan, J.
title: Mind wandering during creative incubation predicts increases in creative performance in a writing task
n: not stated in the record I opened
transfer: none; weak hint that a break helps when the same problem is reused

claim: CHECK: Replication of Baird 2012 (undemanding task + mind wandering boosts Unusual Uses). Verdict: contested, leaning not replicated. Du 2025 (n=85) finds no mind-wandering effect. McDaniel 2025 (preregistered) finds no difference between incubation tasks but a within-person mind-wandering link on same-prompt reuse. I found no study labelled a registered report. A search summary said a preregistered paper states Baird's results did not replicate; I could not open that paper (reCAPTCHA).
authors: Du et al. 2025; McDaniel et al. 2025; Baird et al. 2012
title: Incubation mind-wandering replication status
venue: Brain Sciences; Scientific Reports; Psychological Science
transfer: none; do not build an incubation step on mind wandering

claim: Salmon-Mordekovich and Leikin 2023: insight problem solving resembled spatial non-insight solving, was helped by analogical and convergent thinking with little help from divergent thinking, and was unaffected by secondary tasks. They conclude mostly analytic (business-as-usual) solving, with some evidence of a rare special process.
authors: Salmon-Mordekovich, N.; Leikin, M.
title: Insight problem solving is not that special, but business is not quite 'as usual': typical versus exceptional problem-solving strategies
n: not stated in the record I opened
transfer: an agent may solve most 'insight' puzzles with ordinary analysis; analogy and convergent checking help more than divergence

claim: CHECK: c-09 (most insight problems are solved analytically, impasse about 8%) is partly corroborated by an independent lab (Salmon-Mordekovich and Leikin 2023 find mostly analytic strategy). The 8% figure stays single-source and I did not re-open it. Verdict: direction supported, number unverified. Weisberg's own papers were not opened because the search budget ended.
authors: Salmon-Mordekovich and Leikin 2023
title: Insight problems analytic vs insight solutions
transfer: none

claim: Laukkonen et al. 2021 (preregistered, hand-grip dynamometer): Aha intensity and unintentional squeezing predicted solution accuracy, with a strong positive Aha-accuracy link for problems that demand implicit processing.
quote: a strong positive relationship between Aha moments and accuracy for problems that demand implicit processing
authors: Laukkonen, R. E.; Ingledew, D. J.; Grimmer, H. J.; Schooler, J. W.; Tangen, J. M.
title: Getting a grip on insight: real-time and embodied Aha experiences predict correct solutions
n: not reported in the record I opened
transfer: none; a felt-sudden-confidence signal predicts correctness only for some problem types

claim: Wiley and Miller 2026: Aha ratings are best read as metacognitive judgments. They were highest for solutions with a correct first move, not for solutions needing restructuring, so Aha tracks correctness more than restructuring.
authors: Wiley, J.; Miller, T. S.
title: Aha! Ratings as Metacognitive Judgments
n: not reported in the record I opened
transfer: an Aha-like confidence signal is a cue, not proof; it may fire when the first idea is right

claim: Laukkonen's group also shows Aha can be induced falsely (semantic priming, irrelevant insights), and warnings reduce but do not prevent false Aha moments.
authors: Grimmer, H. J.; Tangen, J. M.; Freydenzon, A.; Laukkonen, R. E.
title: The illusion of insight: detailed warnings reduce but do not prevent false Aha moments
transfer: do not use felt certainty after a sudden answer as a stop rule

claim: CHECK: Aha and accuracy (b-12 vs b-13). Verdict: mixed, not a clean contradiction. Aha predicts accuracy for implicit-processing problems (Laukkonen 2021) and for correct-first-move solutions (Wiley and Miller 2026), yet Aha can be induced falsely and inflates belief in false statements (Laukkonen 2020, Grimmer 2022-23). A Europe PMC search found no meta-analysis of Aha-confidence calibration. Rule: treat Aha as weak, task-dependent evidence.
authors: Laukkonen et al. 2021; Wiley and Miller 2026; Grimmer et al. 2023
title: Aha-accuracy relation
transfer: do not use self-reported sudden confidence as a verifier; use external checks

claim: Preprint: a two-stage prompt (explore the creative space, then satisfy the input requirements), CreativeDC, gave about 1.6 times as many distinct high-utility Python tasks as baselines.
quote: two reasoning stages: (1) exploring the creative space, and (2) satisfying the input requirements
authors: Nguyen, M. H.; Tschiatschek, S.; Singla, A.
title: Enhancing Diversity of LLM-Generated Educational Tasks
transfer: step: explore freely first, then a separate pass applies constraints; fits open-ended tasks only

claim: Preprint: iterative generate-and-select with an LLM scorer reached human-benchmark creativity on recipes, but more iterations alone did not improve creativity, and a smaller in-loop scorer gave higher scores. Evaluator design matters.
quote: additional iterations alone do not improve creativity
authors: Anderson, R.; Verhoef, T.; Zohrehvand, A.
title: Recipes for Creativity: Iterative Generation and Evaluation in Large Language Models
transfer: do not just loop longer; invest in the evaluate step and test which scorer works. Scored by an LLM, so scorer bias applies

claim: Preprint: LLM raters (OCSAI, CLAUS, ChatGPT-4o) scored AI-made Alternate Uses answers higher (self-preference) across 4,813 responses; the bias vanished once idea elaboration was controlled.
quote: Automatic systems tended to privilege artificial responses.
authors: Domanti, U.; Mock, M.; Agnoli, S.; De Angeli, A.
title: The Effect of Idea Elaboration on the Automatic Assessment of Idea Originality
transfer: an LLM judge of ideas is confounded by length and elaboration; control for or equalize elaboration before ranking ideas

claim: Preprint: Haase et al. evaluated 14 LLMs on two creativity tests. They found no clear creative gains over 18 to 24 months, large within-model variability, and only 0.28% of responses reaching the top 10% of human benchmarks.
authors: Haase, J.; Hanel, P. H. P.; Pokutta, S.
title: Has the Creativity of Large-Language Models peaked? An analysis of inter- and intra-LLM variability
transfer: one model varies a lot run to run, so sample many and select; single samples are noisy

claim: Preprint: fMRI of 170 people on the Alternate Uses Task; brain-LLM alignment relates to model size and idea originality, clearest early in the creative process. It does not report a serial-order originality gain for LLMs.
quote: with these relationships clearest early in the creative process
authors: Ismayilzada, M.; Luchini, S. A.; Gokce, A.; et al.
title: Large Language Models Align with the Human Brain during Creative Thinking
transfer: none

claim: CHECK: Serial-order effect in LLMs (later responses more original; b-21 unopened). Verdict: still unverified. Three arXiv API searches on LLM, serial order and Alternate Uses returned zero relevant entries, and I found no paper that tests it. Keep status as human-only. Needs a direct test in our harness: N ideas in one call vs N separate calls, originality scored by position.
authors: n/a
title: Serial order effect in LLM Alternate Uses
transfer: run our own test before adding a 'longer divergent run' step

claim: Preprint: evolutionary persona diversification raised Alternative Uses Task response diversity by 78.8% and originality by 26.1% over task-only prompting.
authors: Moon, S. B.; Cho, N.; Borrajo, D.; Ganesh, S.; Hashemi, A.
title: Breaking Homogeneity: Diversifying Persona Sets for Creative LLM Outputs
transfer: forced divergence via varied personas; matches our NoveltyBench gain, so supports an open-task-only step

claim: CHECK: LLM judges vs humans for novelty. Evidence found is one preprint showing self-preference confounded by elaboration (d-18), plus a humor paper (snippet) saying LLM evaluation criteria favor novelty differently from humans. Not enough to say LLM judges match humans. Verdict: judge bias is real but its source is unsettled.
authors: Domanti et al. 2026; Sakabe et al. 2025
title: LLM judge reliability for novelty
transfer: use a different judge model or a human anchor for novelty ranking; control length
